en: The Commentary on the *Benevolent Kings’ Protection of the Nation Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* Entitled *Shenbao Ji*, Scroll One. [Note:
This sūtra has two titles; its secondary title is "Dragon Jewel King. Herein, I have excerpted these two.
The title is explained by its name; this is said because of the statement that when a Wheel-Turning King appears in the world, divine treasures arrive of their own accord.

Written by the Shramana Bating Shan Yue of Siming, who belongs to the Tiantai school: for this lineage, transmitting the Dharma-lineage is truly the foundation, while the exegesis of the sutras comes second.

However, because he has attained the essence of the Buddha-mind and developed the revolving *dhāraṇī*, whenever he proclaims a sutra or explains a single meaning, it must necessarily be according to the Dharma; thus, he first opens two gates: "An Introductory Discourse on the Great Meaning" and "Exegesis Following the Text."

All major themes must be sought within the initial title, which is further elaborated through the fivefold profound meaning: namely, name (ming), essence (ti), principle (zong), function (yong), and the characteristics of the teaching (jiaoxiang).

Now, every dharma must have a name, and every name must have a substance; substance is its reality, its primary essence, and its seal. If one obtains its seal, it may be trusted and accepted; otherwise, it is merely something heterodox and external.

The "principle" (zong) is the essential means for revealing the essence (ti). By taking cause and effect as the principle, the essence attains its essential core; because the essence is revealed, it possesses function.

When these four elements are fully present and expounded as the teaching, the distinctions between the Small and Great Vehicles, the Partial and Full, the Sudden and Gradual, and the Provisional and Real can be discerned; this is what constitutes their characteristics (xiang).
The details are as stated in such texts as the *Fahua xuanyi* (Profound Meaning of the Lotus Sutra), and so forth.
The passage beginning with "This sutra [is explained] by means of persons and dharmas" below separately enumerates the five meanings of this sutra.
The title is formed by means of "person" and "dharma," referring collectively to both the speaker and the dharma taught.
According to the titles of various sutras appearing below, there are further modes—single, compound, and complete—consisting of three categories: person, dharma, and metaphor, and so forth.

Regarding "taking the true mark as its essence": Generally, all Mahāyāna teachings collectively point to the seal of the one true mark as their essence, which is described in terms of the three virtues.
Since this sutra is titled *Prajñā*, it possesses all three meanings; it correctly corresponds to the true mark, which is precisely the dharma-body of the nature-virtue (*prakṛti-guṇa*).
The essence must necessarily return to unity without departing from its fundamental principle and function; thus, there is the meaning of separation and integration, and so forth.

Regarding the fundamental principle (zong) consisting of the causes and effects of one's own practice: this means that the fundamental principle necessarily exists in relation to practice and possesses cause and effect, and it is precisely this that constitutes the fundamental principle.

Speaking in terms of its pervasive essence, when one is in the state of correct contemplation and observation, then from the initial cause to the final fruit of one's own practice, there is nothing that is not *prajñā*.

While the two wisdoms—the provisional and the ultimate—function as its activity, this activity is fundamentally liberation. Since it correctly corresponds to the *prajñā* of words (*vyañjana-prajñā*), taking "illumination" as its essential meaning, one advances by taking these two wisdoms as its activity.

Regarding the Mahāyāna "ripened butter" as the characteristic of its teaching: this refers to how the various Prajñāpāramitā sections harmonize all dharmas and refine away the two vehicles, manifesting the beneficial characteristics of ripened butter; this is one such instance.

Regarding the title having both general and specific aspects: within this single title, there are twelve characters in total; when including the "Preface" and "Chapter One," it possesses both general and specific aspects, as explained extensively in the text.
Furthermore, it can be understood that the Buddha taught that two characters constitute the general [title], while the remaining characters constitute the specific [title].
Regarding the passage "As for the term 'Buddha'": the following is an exegesis of each part of the title.
This means that the Buddha is the person who speaks; the Buddha possesses ten virtues to manifest the ten epithets.
Awakening (*bodhi*) is the first [of these].
Awakening carries the sense of self-awakening and awakening others to fulfillment; although the objects they confront differ, their nature as awakening is one.

It may also be said that when the three types of awakening reach the perfection of their fruit, one is named a Buddha (*buddha*), and when the eightfold eloquence is proclaimed and circulated, it is called "teaching" (*deśanā*).
The "eight tones" are as explained in the usual commentaries, and so forth.
This is what is meant in the *Awakening of Faith* by the phrase: "The single utterance of the perfect voice is understood differently by various classes of beings.

Below, in the *Benevolent Kings Sutra*, the text clarifies the Dharma being taught; first, the four characters "Benevolent Kings Protecting the State" constitute the essential core that initiates this entire sutra.
"Renwang" (Benevolent King) refers to the sovereign emperors of the Way throughout antiquity and the present.

According to the interpretation provided here, bestowing grace and spreading virtue constitutes "benevolence" (ren), while exercising sovereign transformation and governance constitutes "kingship" (wang); this merely reveals their virtuous function. To exhaustively clarify the Way itself, it cannot be fully encompassed by this alone.
The fourfold commentary on the text:
First, regarding "causes and conditions" (*nidāna*), all matters, meanings, capacities, responses, subjects, and objects are causes and conditions.

As for the term "Protector of the Nation" (*Rāṣṭrapāla*), there is that which protects and that which is protected; generally, this comprises three meanings: [the meaning of the name, the meaning of the function, and the meaning of the result].
First, taking the king as the protector and the kingdom as that which is protected, one governs the state by means of the Way of Kings.
Second, taking Prajñā as the protector and the king as that which is protected, because of upholding Prajñā, both the king and the kingdom attain peace and security.
Third, the King is taken as that which can propagate [the Dharma], and the Dharma as that which is propagated; this is what is meant by "a person can propagate the Way.
Although these three meanings are all applicable, in reality, it is specifically intended to manifest that Prajñā is that which can protect, while the others serve merely as auxiliary explanations.
The phrase "Furthermore, 'Benevolent King' (*Renwang*)" below explains the term through its semantic analysis.

"Benevolent" (*ren*) means "endurance" (*ren*); it also carries the sense of "broad inclusion. This refers to the capacity of one's virtue to be broadly inclusive; thus, rather than immediately giving vent to joy or anger, one's responses invariably accord with the proper measure, thereby manifesting one's benevolence and magnanimity.

Second, regarding the explanation by way of the teachings (*jiao*), the doctrinal system of this school takes the *zang* (Āgama), *tong* (Shared), *bie* (Distinct), and *yuan* (Perfect) as the framework for interpreting the meaning. Therefore, every textual passage and its meaning must be analyzed for its depth or shallowness in relation to these four; thus, the purport of the teaching finds its proper destination, and the understanding of the capacities of sentient beings remains unerring.
If one considers the doctrinal tenets of the ancient and modern schools, there is furthermore the principle of "opening and judging" (kaihan), and so forth.

This text is further divided into four sections, each containing two parts: namely, the explanation of the doctrinal principles according to the teachings, and the word-by-word commentary based on the text.
First, the teachings of the Tripitaka are clarified.
If one perceives the arising and so forth of all phenomena, then the Tripitaka explains arising and cessation.
Phenomena are not identical to emptiness; rather, one must analytically dismantle them to reach emptiness. Thus, arising is existence, and cessation is emptiness.
If it is empty, then dust and all other things can be accommodated; this is the meaning of a "kingdom" (rāṣṭra).
Therefore, remaining unmoving and unchanging, when explained according to the text through topical commentary, the kingdom is secure and the king is at peace.

That which is attained by the two vehicles is called "the King," because the fruit follows from the cause and, in reality, encompasses both cause and fruit; this can be understood by analogy with the [Dharmakāya] lands, and the other three cases follow suit.

It universally explains that all phenomena are such that form itself is emptiness; this differs from the [Sarvāstivāda] analysis of the substance of the storehouse consciousness, and thus they are neither born nor extinguished, all being like illusions and transformations.
"The afflictions of the three realms are severed all at once" is stated from the perspective of the fruit.
If one follows the perspective of the cause, it still allows for gradual severance.

The section beginning with "Abiding outside the realms" is an exegesis based on the text, specifically explaining the sequence of the three truths; it states that the truth of emptiness is not different [from the other two].
Because it penetrates the boundlessness of form, it is "equality" (samā) in its conventional sense;
yet, although it is boundless, it does not obstruct the mind, which is "middle" (madhya).

If one relies on the path of the teachings, this should be the limit; however, to say that the dharma of boundlessness resides within a single moment of mind seems to obstruct the expression of the ultimate meaning.

Now, let us explain this through two points: first, regarding the mind that acts as the creator, it is acceptable even if it is also integrated within the mind; however, regarding the phenomena created by it, they are not so, for it is impossible for them to exist within form.

Secondly, this refers to abiding in the fruit rather than remaining in the cause; as it is said that one enters the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*) in the eighth stage and manifests ten kinds of bodies, this likewise does not contradict the teachings concerning the path of instruction (*śāsana-mārga*).
The section beginning with "From the first stage" provides a commentary on the preceding text.

To say that one is "immovable yet able to move" means that a Bodhisattva of the ten stages in the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra dwells within the ten perfections according to their power and capacity; thus, they possess unimpeded mastery over their practical conduct.
The character "six" (六) is likely an error;
it should be "ten" (十).

Regarding the passage beginning with "If one contemplates" (若觀): because the Perfect Teaching (圓教) explains that all phenomena are fundamentally only the nature of reality (理性), they are without arising or ceasing; this is because, through the Perfect View (圓見), phenomena and principle (事理) are fully present in a single thought-moment.

Although there is no arising or ceasing, arising and ceasing appear vividly; when one loses [the realization of] only arising and ceasing appearing vividly, this is described as "illumination" in terms of the conventional (saṃvṛti). When it is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, this is spoken of as "extinction" in terms of the ultimate (paramārtha).

This also involves illuminating the ultimate and the conventional through the act of illumination, and negating the ultimate and the conventional through the act of negation; thus, negation precedes negation-and-illumination, and illumination precedes negation-and-illumination. When both illumination and negation are found to be unattainable, one accords with the Middle Way.
All three [aspects] accord with the nature (dharmatā), and are therefore as vast as the dharma-nature;
all three are immovable, and are therefore ultimately like empty space.

From the phrase "from the first abode" (*prathamabhūmi*) onwards, the text explains—by way of the partial realization of truth and ultimate perfection—the meanings of dwelling in the land and being called a king.

The passage beginning with "Furthermore, regarding the Tripiṭaka" below generally examines the causes and effects of the four teachings to determine whether the two characters [for "King"] are attained or not.

Thus, the four fruits of the Tripiṭaka are called "Benevolent Kings" because their afflictions have been exhausted; all others have not yet attained this, and though they may be termed "Kings," they lack benevolence.
The Shared Teaching and those that follow all speak from the perspective of the fruit; therefore, it is also appropriate to collectively designate them as "Kings.

The three teachings [of the Śrāvaka, Pratyekabuddha, and Bodhisattva] are merely termed "lesser kings," which refers to the so-called two or three lesser kings who each govern the masses of sentient beings.

Regarding the statement that "each teaching inherently possesses its own degree of superiority or inferiority," this means that when speaking in comparison between them as they each correspond to their respective teachings, the two characters "benevolent" (ren) and "king" (wang) naturally possess a hierarchy of excellence. Therefore, it is said: "If not benevolent, then one is merely a king"—from which the distinction of superiority and inferiority can be understood, and so forth.

Furthermore, speaking from the perspective of worldly governance, there have been those who were benevolent yet did not attain kingship, but there has never been one who attained kingship without being benevolent; those who attained kingship while being unbenevolent were none other than Jie and Zhou.
Regarding the third explanation, that of the primary and secondary manifestations (honji-suijaku), there are two assertions:

namely, that the primary and secondary manifestations of the remote past exist solely within the *Lotus Sūtra*; since even the "trace gate" (jimon) is not yet heard [in other teachings], how much less so the other sections?
Among these traces, one may merely borrow the categories of essence and function, as well as the fundamental and the phenomenal.

This, in turn, briefly unfolds two meanings: first, regarding the fundamental and phenomenal aspects of the partial and the perfect; second, regarding the distinction between the shallow and the deep, wherein the practice of the Perfect is the fundamental and the fruit of the Separate is the phenomenal.
Although the Buddha-ground of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) corresponds to the stage of fruition, it constitutes a "trace" when viewed from the perspective of the Distinct Teaching (Biejiao).

Although the two vehicles of the Tripitaka Teaching (Sanzang) share the same minor fruit, they belong to the "extremity" when viewed from the perspective of the Shared Teaching; "extremity" is synonymous with "trace."
Thus, one knows that when the concepts of "contraction" (*ku*) and "transformation" (*chuan*) are viewed in relation to one another, their meanings are all mutually pervasive.

Alternatively, if discussed according to the specific teachings themselves, each possesses its own "original" (*ben*) and "traced" (*ji*) aspects, such that their meanings do not follow a single standard.
Furthermore, they may be discussed through the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) of the original and the traced, as well as their relative heights and depths, and so forth.

Regarding the fourth, the interpretation through contemplating the mind (*cittāvalokana-vyākhyā*): although the preceding three interpretations are extremely perfect and subtle, they pertain to phenomena (*dharma*) in relation to contemplation; it is only through the practice of perfect contemplation (*pariniṣpanna-avalokana*) within one's own cultivation that their true principle is attained. Therefore, it is said: "It is like a poor man who day and night counts the treasures of others. For this reason, the interpretation through contemplating the mind is necessary.
There are four categories of texts, namely: *samsara* (arising and ceasing), *anutpāda* (non-arising), *apramāṇa* (the immeasurable), and *anabhisaṃskāra* (the unconditioned).

According to the contemplative gateways of the Four Noble Truths, one contemplates objects such as form and emptiness; these differ according to the specific teachings. Thus, it is said that by contemplating the phenomena of arising and ceasing, one perceives that form exists and so forth—this is the contemplation of the *Tripiṭaka* (Śrāvaka vehicle). It means that because arising and ceasing forms are transformed by the mind, the mind attains mastery over them.

The contemplation that "form is itself emptiness" and so forth is a universal contemplation; it is not merely that the mind attains mastery, but because form is itself emptiness, form also attains mastery. Therefore, it is called "the mastery of emptiness and form."
If one contemplates that emptiness is form and enters [the path] in successive stages, this is analytical contemplation (*pratyavekṣā*).
This is what is meant in the *Ratnakūṭa-sūtra* (Yíngluò jīng) when it says that by taking these two contemplations as skillful means, one attains entry into the Middle Way.
If one contemplates that form and emptiness are non-dual, this is the perfect contemplation (*yuánguān*).

Because form and emptiness are fundamentally a single principle through this sudden and perfect approach, from the perspective of illumination, they are non-dual yet dual; yet, while illuminating, they transcend duality and are thus non-dual. This simultaneous illumination and simultaneous transcendence occurs within a single thought-moment; since its essence is the Middle Way, there is nothing that is not the true mark (*shíxiàng*).

The single mind and the three contemplations, the three contemplations and the single mind, are fundamentally without before or after; because it is the single mind and the three contemplations, they are not vertical (sequential), and because the three contemplations are the single mind, they are not horizontal (simultaneous). Being neither vertical nor horizontal, like the Heavenly Eye [of Mount Tiantai], there is nothing more supreme than this wondrous state of mastery.
The passage beginning with "I am now the Holy Lord" is explained by way of contemplating the mind (*cittabhāvanā*).
It attributes the merit to the Sovereign because he transforms through the Way (*mārga*);
it possesses the virtues of a benevolent king because he employs right contemplation (*samyagdṛṣṭi*).

Below this, the meaning of "Protecting the Nation" (Rāṣṭrapāla) is explained in conjunction [with the preceding]. Since the explanation of the "King" has already been briefly clarified as before, and will likewise be detailed later, it is not presented separately here.
Next, the Prajñā is explained.
The term "Prajñāpāramitā" refers to a single scripture that possesses the power to provide protection.
This is because the wisdom and power of Prajñā can ensure the peace and security of a king and cause his governance and transformation to flow forth widely.
These terms are fundamentally untranslatable; among the five principles for not translating found throughout the sūtras and śāstras, this is the first, which one should respect.
The underlying rationale for these untranslated terms is inexhaustible, but I shall now briefly address them in contrast to the ancient treatises.
First, there are two passages cited from the treatise:
one that can be translated, which is the version used by the Kaishan school;

and one that cannot be translated, which is the tradition inherited by Master Min of the Zhuangyan school. Therefore, it is said that "the name contains manifold meanings," which likewise refers to the sense of being "multifaceted" (duōhán).
If one reverses this and relies solely on wisdom, the principle becomes narrow and shallow; yet it is not entirely unacceptable.
Now, in my commentary, I shall first critique these two views and subsequently synthesize them, stating that each has led to contention, which I shall now resolve.
It is said that there are two aspects of Prajñāpāramitā:

first, categorized according to the intent of the various sections, it encompasses both the partial and the perfect, the provisional and the real, and contains meanings of both reversal and non-reversal, thereby harmonizing the doctrines of the two schools.
Although one has not yet rectified the mind, it is possible that this might occur.
Next, the refutation is concluded.

Regarding the statement that "the flame cannot be grasped," as the treatise explains at length: it means that the correct wisdom of *prajñā* cannot be grasped through biased views; to grasp it would be to injure one's hand and harm the reality.
That which cannot be grasped may yet be grasped; though it is grasped, it is permissible.

However, within the interval between grasping and non-grasping, if one does not fall into discursive thought nor engage in deliberation, but directly takes responsibility for it, then there will truly be a point of realization.

The words concerning wisdom admit of both combined and analytical interpretations, and have never been biased toward a single extreme; thus, the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* provides a combined interpretation, while the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* employs an analytical one.
If one follows the interpretation of the sutra, it would mean that knowledge (*jñāna*) has discernment as its nature, while wisdom (*prajñā*) is described by non-attachment.
Because it involves discernment, knowledge is existence; because it involves non-attachment, wisdom is emptiness.
Therefore, when separated, they constitute emptiness and existence; when united, the Middle Way is preserved.
Since this treatise provides a unified interpretation—wherein true wisdom (*tattva-jñāna*) is itself *jñāna*—it is close to *prajñā*; how could there be any fixed abiding therein?
The section beginning with "Now this" below indicates the similarities and differences among the volumes and sections.

According to the later parts of the sutra, the Buddha preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* over twenty-nine years; including what is currently inquired about, it corresponds precisely to the *Benevolent Kings Sutra*, which thus comprises only five sections.
Regarding these eight divisions (*aṣṭau nikāyāḥ*), their origins differ; it must simply be that they vary according to how the volumes were opened or closed, and so forth.
Some say that the *Devarāja* division is identical to the *Benevolent Kings* (*Rājan*) division, but this view is not accepted here.
If they were identical, it would not be necessary to have already taught the *Renwang* [Prajñāpāramitā] and then request it again; therefore, we know they are not the same.
Although there are passages in the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* that share the same name at first glance, this does not mean that the two sections are being spoken of as one.
The section beginning with "Questioning others about benevolence" (*wen ren*) provides a general discussion.
Since benevolence (*ren*) and righteousness (*yi*) are distinct, how can they be considered the same?
Answer:

According to the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*, "benevolence" (*ren*) is precisely what is called "man"; this accords with the statement in the *Book of Documents* that "the person (*ren*) is benevolence (*ren*)," for when these are combined, they constitute the Way (*dao*), and their essential purport is quite similar.

Regarding the passage in the *Laozi* that states, "The sage is not benevolent," the commentary explains that this means the benevolent king practices benevolence without seeking gratitude or reward; it does not mean that he is unbenevolent.
If we speak truly of benevolence and its opposite, then it is simply a matter of whether one follows the Way or not.
Now, when we speak of a "benevolent king," this refers precisely to one who is the master of practicing the Way.
If even an ordinary person is not acceptable when they turn their back on the Way, how much less could such a person be considered benevolent?
He asked again:
"What do you mean by these words, 'benevolent one'?
He replied:
Since benevolence (*ren*) is not easily discussed, let us consider it for a moment by means of its character form.
Thus it is said that "human" (*ren*) is composed of the radical "person" (*ren*) and the number "two" (*er*). These two strokes, when equalized, embody the Way of the Three Powers (*sancai*).
It is further said that "to penetrate the three is to be a king," which is precisely its meaning.
Is this not the explanation of what is called "learning below and attaining above"?
He asked again:
Ancient scholars considered this sutra to be a non-canonical translation because it was not found in the catalogs.
The gist of the response is that the presence or absence of a text in a catalog likely results from accidental omission.
As for the three translations that appeared later, how could they not be authentic?
Moreover, since the *Chángfáng Mùlù* (Catalogue of Chángfáng) is available for consultation, it is clear that this is not a false attribution.
Below the entry for "Hǎiyōng," he cites historical events to refute the error.

That is to say, the commoners of the seas and the sages of antiquity both conjectured about existence or non-existence regarding things beyond the reach of their ears and eyes; how could they have known the actual reality?
The character *gé* (革) may also be pronounced *jí* (棘); this is evidenced by the passage in the *Liezi*, etc. Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, according to...

(*qiě zhǔn*) and below, [the author] correctly presents the extensive and abridged versions and the three translations in their respective orders to clarify their authenticity; yet, the fault of one who composes such a critique is none other than extreme.

However, as for the fact that the commentary alone is based on the Qin translation among the three versions, it is because compared to the other two versions, Kumārajīva’s translation is superior; its phrasing and reasoning are both fluent and comprehensive, and it was thus revered by the people of the time.

"Pāramitā" translates as "the completion of an undertaking," and it also translates as "reaching the other shore"; both manifest the supreme function of *prajñā*. This means that when an undertaking is completed, its underlying principle becomes known.

Of the six perfections, the first five pertain to phenomena (*dharma*), while Prajñā-pāramitā pertains to principle (*li*). If even phenomena, when guided by principle, lead to the ultimate, how much more so when principle itself acts as the guide—could it not be the ultimate?

To speak of "reaching the other shore" is like using a boat or raft to cross the great ocean; there are distinctions between this shore, that shore, and the middle of the stream. Remaining on this shore or in the middle is not yet ultimate; only upon reaching the other shore is one's task fulfilled.
These are all meanings that reach the ultimate; therefore, it is said that "birth and death constitute this shore," and so forth.
Although this is an exegesis based on specific textual passages, its meaning remains generally applicable and pertains to the nature of dependent origination.

Next, regarding the explanation by way of the teachings (*yōkyō*): in the *Hīnayāna* (Tripitaka), taking the real existence of birth-and-death as "this" and the extinction of existence in *nirvāṇa* as "that," the delusions of view and thought constitute the middle current.

What is expounded belongs to the Small Vehicle; since all six *pāramitās* are merely matters of practice and have not yet attained the ultimate reaching of the shore, the eightfold noble path among the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipakṣadharma*) is taken as the raft.
In the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao), this and that are no different from the Tripiṭaka; however, because it explains the analysis of substantial entities, the Six Perfections constitute its principle.
If compared to the Tripiṭaka, then both the phenomena and the principle therein are all phenomena, whereas here, both phenomena and principle are principle—this is the distinction.

Since ignorance is designated as the "middle current" in this alternative exposition, it logically follows that the form and emptiness of ordinary beings and *śrāvakas* constitute this [current], which belongs to the internal realm;
the provisional dharmas of Bodhisattvas constitute that [other shore], which belongs to the external realm;
and immeasurable practices and vows serve as the boat and oars.

In the Perfect and Sudden teaching, this is the ultimate. Speaking in terms of phenomena and principle: when phenomena reach their ultimate, they are identical with principle—thus "two yet not two"; when principle reaches its ultimate, it is identical with phenomena—thus "not two yet two. By analogy, the relationship between birth-and-death and nirvana as "this" and "that" can be understood through this same logic.

In reality, however, there is neither birth-and-death nor nirvana to be attained; yet by employing this to assist one's practice, a single practice becomes all practices, serving as a boat or raft to ultimately reach the shore of Great Nirvana—this is what is meant.

Next, regarding the interpretation of "the other shore" (*pāra*) through the contemplation of the mind: it does not go beyond the application of the [Three Truths of] Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle, taking the emptiness of form and so forth as the meaning of "this" and "that.
As for the method of cultivation, this is the gate of contemplation based on phenomena (*shikishō kanmon*), as explained at length in the text.
The meaning of the "three provisional designations" (trividha-prajñapti) will be explained later.
Regarding the phrase "the sūtra exists," this explains the meaning of the word *sūtra*.
In Sanskrit it is called *sūtra*; in older translations, it was said to have a literal equivalent (*yǒu fān*) or to be without a literal equivalent (*wú fān*).

The five categories, such as the "historical thread" (lìguàn xiàn), each consist of three meanings—teaching, practice, and principle—resulting in fifteen meanings in total, as explained in detail in the *Xuánshì* (Commentary on the Profound Meaning) and so forth.
Furthermore, the term "sūtra" (jīng) is glossed as "dharma" and "eternal," and it also carries the meaning of "warp and woof."
Furthermore, regarding the "sūtras" of the Six Classics, they are called "sūtras" simply because they serve as a constant standard to replace [erroneous views] with the correct.
In the section beginning with "Defining the six sense-objects according to the teachings," the author again uses the sūtras to clarify the essence of the teaching.
Now, the Sūtra is that by which the Sage provides instruction.
Through this instruction, one awakens to the Way; thus, there is both the universal and the particular.
"Universal" means that throughout the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, all six sense objects are the substance of the teaching, as stated in various passages of the text.
Alternatively, by means of light and so forth, the Buddha performs his work by fully enumerating the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*).

In the case of the fragrant food, it naturally encompasses three sense objects: "fragrance" refers to the object of smell (*gandhaviṣaya*); once the food enters the mouth, its continuous and subtle flavor is the object of taste (*rasaviṣaya*); and the sensations of softness, sweetness, and so forth experienced between the lips and tongue are the object of touch (*spraṣṭavyaviṣaya*).
Or, one may attain samādhi through silent stillness and wordlessness, which is precisely the object-field of dharmas (*dharmaviṣaya*).
Extending this principle further, each and every sense-object (*viṣaya*) possesses all six sense-faculties (*indriya*), and each and every sense-faculty likewise possesses all six sense-objects.
Throughout the entire Dharma-realm, every faculty and every object can serve as an entry point to the Path; thus, what could possibly fail to be the essence of the teaching?

This applies analogously to all cases, such as the classification of teachings (*yàojiào*), the fundamental and the manifested (*běnjì*), and the contemplation of the mind (*guānxīn*). So it goes on and on.

Even if one speaks of the essential heart-transmission outside the teachings, reaching the state of no words and no characters, as long as there is even a single dharma that either accords with the mind or does not accord with the mind, this too is the essence of the teaching; where and what dharma could then be considered a "separate transmission"?
Were it not for one who deeply perceives this principle, it would be difficult to express through pen or tongue.

Specifically, [the Sarvāstivāda] takes sound and form as its essence, distinguishing between the period when the Buddha was in the world and after his parinirvāṇa; furthermore, it posits that the three—name, phrase, and syllable—are the "one reality," while the three [realities] combine through convention to form the essence. Thus, its teaching is complete.

Regarding the three provisional designations that praise its qualities, such as "the provisional designation of sensation" (*vedanā-prajñapti*) and so forth: first, the essence is indicated and the name is explained.
