To say that [a phenomenon] lacks intrinsic substance itself yet exists by depending on others refers to the reason for its being provisional; this is what is meant in the *Mohe Zhiguan* by the phrase "arising without a master."
Furthermore, the statement that "one is named 'empty' and two are named 'real' by way of mutual relation" explains the distinction between the empty and the real.
However, when it says "only real yet empty," it should properly be stated as "real-empty"; this is merely a conventional expression used for the purpose of generalizing and indicating the conclusion.
Considering that its substance is empty, this very reality is what constitutes illusion; because it is illusory, it fulfills the meaning of "penetration" (tong).

Within each of the three provisional designations (sanyajia), there are three contemplations (sanguan); these are explained here by applying the aforementioned distinctions to the three contemplations.

That "the provisional nature of phenomena is itself emptiness" means that because phenomena are empty, they are unreal; because they are unreal, they are empty—this is the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

That "emptiness is itself the reality of the provisional" means that, in contrast to the provisional name, what is real is not truly real; the locus of reality is itself emptiness. Therefore, while a single form or a single fragrance fundamentally belong to the realm of the provisional, because their essence is empty, there is nothing that is not *prajñā*.
Because it is identical with principle, emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is merely provisional; this is the contemplation of the provisional (*jia-guan*).

As for the character "contemplation" (*guan*), it refers to the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*): within it there is an essence that is neither empty nor provisional, yet it possesses the function of being able to be both empty and provisional. Thus, emptiness and the provisional serve as skillful means (*upāya*) to enter the Middle Way.

Because the middle supersedes the extremes, these two extremes possess only their names and cannot be called "contemplation"; it is only by virtue of the reality of the middle that one may finally speak of them.
This is all explained by way of provisional designations based on phenomena (*dharma*).
The subsequent two contemplations may be understood by analogy, and so forth.

If one clarifies the perfect contemplation (*yuan-guan*) by means of the three provisional designations (*san-jia*), there is no separate "perfection" apart from the sequence; rather, through successive stages, one integrates [the phenomena] back into the single mind as emptiness, the provisional, and the middle, whereby they naturally vanish and are illuminated, and thus perfection is attained.
In the second fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, three sections are established to explain [the subject] through parables.
First, two parables are set forth; the meaning of the first, "a dog approaching a well," is easily understood.
The character "chì" (叱) should be read as "fèi" (吠, barking); furthermore, the two characters "xiàngyǐng" (相影) are likely inverted.

The passage beginning with “Sentient beings are also like this” constitutes the synthesis (*saṃgraha*), which still encompasses three meanings—namely, the conventional nature of phenomena (*dharma-prajñapti*) and so forth—as explained in detail in the text.

Furthermore, regarding the point that all phenomena merely arise from the conjunction of names and are designated as “body” and so forth, and that there is no other name: this means there is no distinct name [apart from these designations].
One should also formulate the following method: namely, that there are no distinct phenomena within the three realms, but only provisional designations.
It should be understood that all such cases—such as "substance," "name," "part," and so forth—are likewise based on actual phenomena.
The section beginning with "The three emptinesses, etc. explains the praise for the virtues of samādhi.
Because one penetrates emptiness by means of the conventional, the three emptinesses are praised next; this also follows the sequence of cause and effect.
This means that because phenomena are merely conventional designations, they are empty, and so forth; the meaning can be understood through such [explanations].

Regarding the phrase "Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*," it cites the treatise to clarify that the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) are the gates for proceeding toward *nirvāṇa*. Thus, the factors of the path (*mārgāṅga*) are the means by which one proceeds, serving as the gate for proceeding toward the destination of *nirvāṇa*.
Furthermore, it is said that there are three gates to nirvāṇa, which are the three emptinesses.

Moreover, as these serve as the gates for proceeding toward nirvāṇa, one should establish the meaning of two successive gates: the outer gate consists of the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma), while the inner gate consists of the three emptinesses.
This is precisely why the inner sanctum of the Tathāgata’s hall of the three virtues of great nirvāṇa bliss is even more profound.
The passage beginning with "As for what is called the gate of emptiness" is a restatement followed by an explanation.

This means that by contemplating that all phenomena are without self or what belongs to a self, one removes their obscurations; since they exist through the combination of causes and conditions, one realizes the conditions of phenomena, and that which serves as the master or locus is itself empty.
The absence of both agent and recipient is what is called "primordially empty.
It is for these three reasons that it is termed the "Gate of Emptiness" (śūnyatā-mukha).
As for the "Gate of Signlessness" (animitta-mukha), it means that although one contemplates the body as empty, one still experiences the Gate of Emptiness.

Yet, because there remains the presence of marks (*nimitta*), one must apply the antidote to attachment to marks by cultivating the markless (*animitta*). As it is said, bending, stretching, bowing, and looking up—all such things are what are called "marks.
Marks are fundamentally without reality; that which moves and shifts is wind (*vāyu*). Wind depends upon consciousness (*vijñāna*) to perform its functions.
If consciousness were to cease, then because it would not exist from moment to moment, how could there be any marks?
Where there are no marks, there is no self.
Yet, seeing such marks as male and female is due to the presence of a self-centered mind and a lack of wisdom; thus, one falsely perceives such marks as the interconnected chain of bones.
What is called "skin and bone covering a mechanism that moves" is like a wooden puppet; this is as described in detail in the *Liezi*.
Regarding the "Gate of Non-action": all created things depend upon the signless (*animitta*); yet if even the signless does not exist, how could there be anything created?
Therefore it is said: "The signless is also the absence of such names; this is the unconditioned.

These three gates of emptiness are the essentials among all meditations (*dhyāna*). If one lacks these concentrations, they are not called *samādhi*; because [such states] easily lead to many regressions and losses, it is said that only three types of people can reach *nirvāṇa*: namely, those who uphold the precepts, those who contemplate emptiness, and those who are diligent.
When these three conditions are present, more than half of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment have already been accomplished.
By means of the first gate, one attains the three liberations; then the second gate can be undertaken, and one’s departure from the secret treasury will not be far off.
The concluding summary and praise following the Four Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination can be understood as such.

If one were to treat the Truths and the Links as two separate sections, it would seem unnecessarily redundant; moreover, since the subsequent passage praising the Pratyekabuddhas also contains these same phrases, why should they not be analyzed and explained here?

However, regarding the Truths (satya), Bases (āyatana), and Paths (mārga) and so forth, when categorized according to the [Three] Pitakas, there are differences in their expansion and contraction based on whether one's faculties are sharp or dull.

Since the present [teaching] belongs to the Universal Vehicle (pāramitā-yāna), these can be integrated into a single unity; thus, there are both commonalities and distinctions, as explained extensively in the Commentary (śāstra).

Furthermore, the statement "the Four Truths are for those of dull faculties to contemplate" includes both those of sharp and dull faculties who contemplate based on subsequent causes and conditions; thus, there is both a general and a specific application.

When the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra* (or *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra*) is consulted, each [truth] applies to all four teachings; therefore, the application according to the specific text and its meaning do not follow a single uniform standard.
The second row consists of the assembly of *pratyekabuddhas*.
Regarding the term "Great Sages (*maharṣi*) who are *pratyekabuddhas*," there are three designations for their status: namely, first, the *pratyekabuddhas* and so forth.

Although they are fundamentally listed as *pratyekabuddhas*, they are here referred to as "Great Sages" because this uses the external to illustrate the internal; taking their awakening to be the same, they are thus designated by that title.
The second are the pratyekabuddhas, who are those currently listed among the assembly of listeners.
Although they appeared during the Buddha’s lifetime, how do they differ from those who attain solitary awakening to the non-arising of phenomena?
The principles of non-annihilation and non-permanence, and so forth, are generally explained by way of three meanings.
Taken collectively, because things arise through conditions they are not annihilated; because conditions cease, they are not permanent.
The virtues extolled as being neither annihilated nor eternal are hereby exhausted.
As for the three types of *pratyekabuddhas*—also called *ekabuddhas*—there are both similarities and differences between them.
They are similar in that they appear in eras devoid of a Buddha; they differ in that their faculties vary, resulting in the distinction between the "small" and the "great."

Because they do not produce great uncontrolled fruits, they are exclusively those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*); yet, as they still abide in the causal stage, they remain persons in training (*śaikṣa*).
The root-nature (*indriya-gotra*) of the Pratyekabuddha is somewhat difficult to clarify; such is the general outline, and so forth.
The critical analysis has two layers:
first, the question encompasses two meanings.
That is to say, if the three vehicles were entirely distinct, it would not be the case that the truths and conditions are explained separately in both places.
Next, the Bodhisattvas are listed, yet they are still called Arhats.
If they were entirely identical, how would the Three Vehicles be distinguished?
The answer is: they differ in the manner of attaining enlightenment regarding the same object.

This means that while they universally rely on the truths and their objects as being fundamentally the same realm, they differ according to individual capacities; thus, their modes of understanding and realization are not uniform, which is why they are likened, for instance, to the three animals crossing a river, and so forth.
The passage beginning with “Therefore, the Great Sūtra” below cites commonality to prove distinction.
Because the objects [of perception] are the same, one universally contemplates causes and conditions; because the realization is distinct, the attainment of bodhi differs.
One should also include the fourfold sets of the Four Noble Truths, as discussed extensively above.
The section beginning with "It is truly because" concludes the core meaning and provides the response; this may be understood accordingly.

Next, the intent of the question is: since the Great Sages (Maharṣis) and Pratyekabuddhas originally appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, why are they now listed among the assembly of those who hear the teaching together?
Since the term "pratyekabuddha" does not appear in the sūtra, the question is addressed using the general term "pratyayabuddha.
The answer states that pratyayabuddhas also exist during the lifetime of a Buddha, but they are subsumed within the category of śrāvakas.
Regarding the statement that Pratyekabuddhas appear in worlds where no Buddha exists, this refers specifically to the *pratyekabuddha* (solitary realizer).
As for the listing of the Bodhisattva assembly as fivefold, it is as explained in the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings), and so forth.
The "Great Path Mind" (mahābodhicitta), as spoken of today, refers to the full accomplishment of all merits, including both ultimate wisdom (jñāna) and skillful means (upāya).
A "Great Being" (mahāsattva) is also called an "Opening Being" (kai-shi), meaning one who is able to sustain great undertakings and open up the Way of the Dharma.

Regarding the statement within the provisional teachings that the mind is superior while the path is inferior: because the bodhisattva places others before themselves and is earnest in benefiting sentient beings, they are superior to the śrāvaka.

However, since this refers to the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* and one hundred kalpas of the *āgama* (Tripitaka) stage, where the severing of afflictions has not yet been discussed, they are inferior to the arhat.

Although the *Abhisamayālaṃkāra* and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtras* differ as separate collections (*piṭaka*), their teachings do not involve artificial fabrication; therefore, it is said that they "retain the residual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
Since these tendencies do not arise independently, it is said that they "support the vows" (*praṇidhāna*).
This is why they are distinct.

Regarding the statement, "One should know that when the practices of the ten stages are perfected, one is like a Buddha": because the tenth stage is also called a "bodhisattva," it receives the designation "like" (tathā).
This means that it is equal to the Buddha of the ultimate teaching.

Regarding "neither accomplished nor unaccomplished": when one contemplates the non-dual realm with a mind of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are non-active and thus not accomplished; yet, because they are perfectly realized in a single thought-moment, they are not unaccomplished.
The section beginning with "Now this" concludes and judges the meaning of the bodhisattvas listed previously.
This current point properly corresponds to the initial gateway of the Mahāyāna teaching; it is the ten stages of common practice (*sādhāraṇa-caryā-bhūmi*).

Upon reaching the eighth stage, there is a sense of both "inclusive" (*jian*) and "distinct" (*bie*), because it correctly and inclusively connects [the stages]; thus it is called "secretly inclusive" (*mijian*), which is not the same as the "secret" (*mi*) of the "exoteric and esoteric" (*xianmi*).

If one relies on the three types of arousal of the mind (*citta-utpāda*) according to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, then the meanings elucidated by each of the three teachings should also be understood as inclusive; thus, both explanations are acceptable.
"All are arhats" clarifies the stage of the bodhisattva.
Since bodhisattvas of the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* have not yet severed their afflictions, they are not called arhats; it is only upon reaching the fruit that they may be so designated.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "those who practice the fundamental conduct," there are two meanings in the text:

first, it refers to obtaining the name based on a bodhisattva reaching the fruit; second, it refers to the Tathāgata’s direct application of minor transformation, wherein he temporarily conforms [to them] to provide authentication. Thus it is said.
As for the latter two flavors, they ought to be discarded; how could there be anything [of value] in them?
Regarding the bodhisattvas of the three teachings, their status is evaluated according to the text.

Furthermore, the passage from the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* is cited as proof, stating that this is the establishment of a distinct name for the "patience" (kṣānti) of bodhisattvas. This is also intended to praise the bodhisattvas and to encourage the advancement of those of the two vehicles.
However, previously, regarding the Śrāvakas, it was clarified that they are all Arhats, meaning there is no distinction between those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa).
Now, regarding the Bodhisattvas, there is both inclusion and exclusion; what is the intention behind this?
In the answer, it is explained that there is no fixed standard for the form of a bodhisattva.
Now, I maintain that while this is certainly one interpretation, it is not without further meaning.

Previously, based on the śrāvakas who consist only of those in training (śaikṣa) and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), [the term] was applied to all because they progress from the stage of training to the stage beyond training.

Now, it is clarified that since the Bodhisattva has already traversed both the Separate and Perfect Teachings, there are subsequent stages to be expected; therefore, the inclusion and exclusion are discussed in contrast between the True and the Provisional.
That the commentary does not mention this is merely due to brevity.
The section beginning with "Question: If... explains and further clarifies the underlying reason.

This means that since it has now been clarified that the physical appearance and attire of a Bodhisattva are universal, they might at times coincide with those of ordinary people or followers of the Lesser Vehicle, thereby failing to avoid confusion; therefore, it is explained once more so that one may know there is a specific standard for both advancing and retreating [in practice].

This means that for those who hold the Hinayana in high esteem, it is to make them realize that the virtues of the Great and Small Vehicles are equal, thereby encouraging them to advance toward the Great Vehicle.

For those who cling to names and characteristics, it is to awaken them to the transcendence of the paths of ordinary beings and sages, thereby causing them to retreat from the state of an ordinary person.
Therefore, this is explained again with emphasis.
Next, the remaining meanings are presented.
From the section "The Merits of Real Wisdom" onwards, there are eleven topical divisions; among these, the virtues of wisdom are first extolled.
There is ultimate wisdom and there is skillful means wisdom.
Ultimate wisdom illuminates emptiness; this is the essence of prajñā.
Skillful means wisdom illuminates existence; this is the function of prajñā.
As clarified in the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* regarding the fourfold propositions on the bondage and liberation of true wisdom and skillful means, this is close to the present case, and so forth.

Below the section "The Previous Clarification of the Stages," there is a reiteration of the clarification of the stages, explaining the reasons for both the shared and distinct aspects of praising their virtues.

Now, if we correlate the seventh and eighth stages of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao) with the two types of wisdom, then because the seventh stage corresponds to the level of the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), it constitutes real wisdom (bhūta-jñāna); beyond this, it is expedient wisdom (upāya-jñāna).
If this is not explained by way of the meaning of being "received" (*pratigraha*), what else could it mean?
Those who practice the Mahāyāna alone praise it as being distinctively that which Bodhisattvas ride.
Since the two vehicles have no share in it, it is said to be "exclusively Mahāyāna," and so forth.
Regarding the fourth point, the praise of the eyes: one should fully clarify the five eyes, noting the differences between their presence and absence.

When a bodhisattva is on the causal path, as long as the stages of practice have not yet been perfected, they possess only four eyes; because they have not yet attained the ultimate fruit, they do not yet possess the Buddha-eye.
However, when inferred according to the meaning of "being like a Buddha," the common eye should also be complete;
for although the initial mind of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching possesses only the fleshly eye, because its understanding is superior, it is called the Buddha-eye.
Regarding the phrase "now, within the ten stages of faith," this means that one further advances by means of what resembles realization.

Next, concerning the praise of the supernormal powers (abhijñā), following the analogy of the eye, there are only five; because they defer to the ultimate fruit, they do not reach six. Whether they advance or not is as explained above, and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the one with the three penetrations" (*trividya*) below: among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), the clear penetration of the three periods of time is called the "three knowledges.
There is a textual error of one character, "lai" (來).
As for the "ten powers" (*daśabala*), they are listed in full as in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

Regarding the power of not being weary of birth and death therein: it is precisely because one possesses the remaining nine powers, and moreover, due to the absence of self, that one does not grow weary of birth and death; thus, there is no power greater than this.
The followers of the Two Vehicles lack this power; therefore, they cannot escape their fear and seek liberation.
As for the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*), they are called "immeasurable" because the mind that takes them as its object is vast and expansive.
This is originally the Brahma-faring (*brahmacarya*); now, praising the Bodhisattva, this too is the virtue of a Bodhisattva.

Even if one possesses the aforementioned three [virtues], if one has not yet been able to relinquish what is not yet wholesome, one can only achieve non-attachment toward both self and others; this is the ultimate practice. Therefore, the commentary states at length.
The characteristics, names, and meanings of the remaining dharmas may be understood according to the *Dharmadhātuanupūrvī*.
"The Vajra-extinguishing Samādhi" praises the virtue of abandonment (*prahāṇa*).
While the preceding sections mostly pertain to wisdom (*jñāna*), these constitute the two virtues of wisdom and abandonment.

"Wisdom" (jñāna) refers to the severing of afflictions by means of wisdom; "severance" (prahāṇa) refers to the realization attained through that severance. Specifically, the term "wisdom" denotes the virtue of the path of non-obstruction (*ānantarya-mārga*), while the term "severance" denotes the virtue of the path of liberation (*vimukti-mārga*).
It is further said: "The virtue of wisdom is the actual severance through severance," meaning that by means of wisdom, there is actually something severed.
"The virtue of severance is non-severance as severance," meaning that if one does not sever, it is already severed; there must be realization, and this realization also arises because of severance.
This principle is even more difficult to clarify.
Furthermore, as for the term "severance" (*duàn*), its upper tone signifies "to cut off. To sever so that there is no continuation is the meaning of severance.
Moreover, in Perfect Enlightenment, neither subject nor object can be found; as it is said, "Since the head has already been severed, there is no one who severs," and thus it is likened to a vajra.
The principle is this: meditative concentration (*samādhi*) is able to shatter afflictions while its own essence remains unmoved.
*Śūraṅgama* translates as "heroic aspect" (*kṣānti-lakṣaṇa*), meaning that its intrinsic nature is courageous and robust, being uniquely capable of subduing Māras and overcoming adversaries.
The passage beginning with "Furthermore, there were thousands of myriads of kotis" lists three categories of miscellaneous assemblies.
In total, there are four:
first, humans; second, gentlemen; third, devas; and fourth, worthies.
The division of the text and its translation can be understood [from the preceding].
In the passage where "worthy ones" (xián) appears, the character was erroneously written as "people" (rén).

Regarding the formal explanation of the five precepts: it refers to abstaining from killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth; it merely guards the body and speech without mentioning mental karma (*manas-karman*), for by citing the branches one may understand the root.

Regarding the single precept against drinking alcohol which universally prevents two types of misconduct: this is stated in brief without explicitly stating the underlying intention, as it refers back to what was said above.

Its meaning is also explained as above; this pertains to the Human Vehicle (*puruṣayāna*), and the question of whether or not it prevents [misconduct] according to the Small or Great Vehicles has not yet been discussed.
If one departs from the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*), then that is the vehicle of the devas (*devayāna*).

As for the citation of the passage concerning Trapusa and Bhallika: this refers to the time when the Buddha had first attained enlightenment but had not yet turned the wheel of Dharma; he provisionally taught the Dharma of the five precepts to these two men in accordance with their own prior inclinations, hence there is the text of the present dialogue.

The five precepts possess clarity; they are neither four nor six. Vast and all-encompassing, there is nothing they do not include. Thus, there are eight matters, such as the five stars, each corresponding one-to-one with these [precepts], and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "by not killing" and below: when the five precepts are assigned to the five directions, the east belongs to wood; wood presides over benevolence (*ren*). Since benevolence takes the nourishing of life as its foundation, "not killing" is assigned to it.
Other precepts are similar to this, as stated in various texts.

If one relies on the principles of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, then upholding and violating the precepts—provided they are understood through their essential meaning—are all none other than the Perfect Vehicle, as explained in detail in the *Guanwuliangshoujing Shu* (Commentary on the Amitābha Sūtra).

However, although this sutra was preached at the beginning [of the Buddha’s career], it is not of the initial teaching; because the Three Jewels were not yet complete, it is not the fundamental teaching for transcending the world. Therefore, it is appropriate that it bestows the Small Vehicle while simultaneously encompassing and gathering in those on the periphery.

In the past, those who did not understand established this as the primary teaching for humans and devas; consequently, it was refuted by the seven points of our present school, as fully detailed in the *Xuánwén* and explained at length in other chapters, and so forth.
"Adjacent to the Sages" refers to the "Worthy.
Furthermore, regarding those called "provisional practitioners," this is said because they are explained in contrast to the Worthy and Sages; thus, they are termed "adjacent to the Sages.

From the perspective of their outward traces, they are currently engaged in preliminary matters and have not yet attained the status of one who practices contemplation; therefore, they are designated by the term "provisional," which is equivalent to a mere name.

Regarding the phrase "all practicing as arhats": if this [title] is placed above the following [text], it indicates that the stages of the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) and the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), etc., are all dharmas to be cultivated. Thus, one knows that although their outward traces are the same as those of ordinary beings, their fundamental nature is that of arhats, bodhisattvas, and so forth.

Whether this progression or regression can be easily assessed is difficult to determine; in short, it is simply a matter of participating in the Buddha’s sublime assembly, such that its fundamental reality (*hon*) and its manifested traces (*saku*) cannot be debated.
Regarding the passage "The Ten Stages have three kinds," the various sources from the sutras and treatises differ.
Were it not for the distinct demarcation provided by the tenets of this specific school, who could clarify its applications and the depth of its stages?

Regarding the three types [of ten stages], the first consists of the ten stages practiced in common by the three vehicles; these correspond to the general positions and are explained as they are commonly enumerated.

Secondly, as clarified in the *Mahā-śāstra*, there are two kinds of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-jñāna*): first, the stage of dry wisdom of the śrāvaka, which is the aforementioned common practice; since its stages of practice and merits are entirely identical to those of the Tripiṭaka [teachings], it is called "śrāvaka."

Practicing solely for the sake of *nirvāṇa*, all that one cultivates and practices is for the purpose of self-deliverance; this distinction lies merely in the general and the specific: either practicing the *buddhānusmṛti-samādhi* as the primary contemplation, or practicing the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) and so forth as auxiliary contemplations.

However, all of these are beginners with shallow practice who have not yet attained the water of concentration and principle; though they possess slight wisdom, it has not yet become integrated with their being. Therefore, they are called those of "dry wisdom," and so forth.

The section beginning with "Regarding the bodhisattva" below clarifies the ten stages of the bodhisattva, such as the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). This refers to what the text calls "the bodhisattva from the first production of the thought of enlightenment until not yet attaining the patient acceptance of conformity (*anulomikī-kṣānti*). When distinguished specifically, these correspond to the ordinary beings (*bāhyapṛthagjana*) of the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*).
The following two categories are both explained by alternating between specific and general characteristics, as can be seen from the text itself.

Regarding the phrase "up to the Bodhisattva grounds," all stages from the first, the Ground of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), up to the Ground of Dharma Clouds (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) are termed "Bodhisattva"; this is an instance of using a specific name to denote the general category.

Speaking from this perspective, the separate establishment of the name "patience" (kṣānti) was originally intended for its distinct stage; yet it is borrowed here as a general designation because, in the case of Bodhisattvas, each possesses the virtue of patience that surpasses that of the two vehicles. This, too, reflects the intent of the Mahāyāna to refine and purify.
If one did not borrow the term "position" (wei) to designate it, then [the categories] would be conflated and indistinguishable.
As for other matters, they are as explained in texts such as the *Xuanyi* and the *Zhiguan*; thus, we know that this school’s practice of borrowing meanings is indeed profound in its intent.

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha-ground" (*buddhabhūmi*) and so forth: it is because the aforementioned bodhisattvas have fulfilled the merits of both self and others during the causal stage (*hetubhūmi*) that, upon reaching the fruit, they achieve the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*), whereby it is designated by the name "Buddha-ground."

If one speaks of the distinct and perfect [teachings] regarding the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), their beginning and end are fundamentally those of a bodhisattva, not shared with those of the two vehicles; their positions are clearly delineated and need not be borrowed from others.
However, when discussing the distinct teaching on its own terms, it still retains the path of doctrinal instruction, and thus there is the doctrine of "separated and successive" progression.

Only the perfectly realized path is exclusively and completely harmonious; therefore, the commentary provides these various explanations to distinguish it. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "dedicating [merit] toward the fivefold Dharma-body":

if one were to discuss dedication according to its fundamental stage, it should belong to the stage prior to the grounds (*bhūmi-pūrva*). Yet, here it is instead listed after them as a praise of dedication. The sub-commentary explains this by way of a distinct transition, ensuring that one does not stagnate in emptiness but returns to the Middle Way; this is precisely the meaning of dedication.
The section beginning with "Endowment of Speech" addresses the previous deficiency in the fivefold aspects of partial truth; it is now provided so that they may be fulfilled.

These five aspects do not exceed the three bodies: namely, the first four parts constitute the Body of Merit (*guṇakāya*), while knowledge and vision constitute the Body of Wisdom (*jñānakāya*). Since these together adorn the Dharma-body of intrinsic virtue (*dharmakāya*), the three bodies are perfectly complete, and their underlying meaning becomes even more manifest.
Regarding dedication for the sake of wholesome benefit, I shall now briefly set forth two types: namely, dedicating oneself toward others and dedicating causes toward the fruit.
Since the fruit must reach the ultimate, the principle of dedicating phenomena toward the noumenon is thereby encompassed.

The *Tanshengxinü* (Praise of the Pure Faith Woman) also states that she possesses the merits of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*). This text initiates the teaching of "three births" within each of the ten stages; it does not merely present the beginning, middle, and end as traversing the ten stages to collectively constitute thirty births—namely, the "increasing of the Path and diminishing of births"—but rather asserts that a single stage encompasses the merits of all stages.

Furthermore, it is said that one on the first stage does not know the lifting and setting down of the feet of one on the second stage; yet, as for the "skillful entry, exit, and abiding" cited here, their meanings are not uniform. Thus we know that the principle of the Perfect and Sudden Dharma-gate is inexhaustible.
Within the praise of the householder’s virtues, the statement that "there are two among the seven worthies" is as it appears in the text.
However, regarding all practices undertaken prior to the stages (bhūmi), there are none that are not termed "harmonizing the mind and conforming to the Way."
"If the mind is not harmonized, the Way will not be followed; if the Way is not followed, the Sage has no means of entry—these words are exhaustive.

These names and characteristics of the Seven Worthies of the Mahāyāna differ slightly [from other traditions]. I have not yet verified whether foreigners refer to one who has accumulated wealth to the extent of a hundred million as a *gṛhapati* (lay devotee), which would be far removed from the "seven pure riches" possessed by Vimalakīrti.
Now, seeing that many people in the world nowadays value such titles, is this not nearly excessive and profane?
Regarding those whose virtue and conduct are fully perfected, "virtue" is itself "conduct," and it also constitutes "the conduct of virtue"; for now, I shall explain according to the former sense.

The meaning may also be understood such that this phrase serves as the general heading, while the subsequent virtues constitute the particulars; that is to say, there are twenty-two categories in total, comprising eight sections, with the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*) consisting of four [sections], and so forth.

Only the category of the "stages" (*avasthā*) consists of twenty-two factors; this excludes the seven factors of enlightenment and the eightfold noble path, which belong to the path of vision (*darśanamārga*), as the remaining categories precede it.

Regarding the names and characteristics of the various sections such as the ten totalities (*kṛtsnāyatana*), they are fully detailed in the *Dharmadhātuvyavasthāna* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm), and so forth.

Question: Regarding the eight liberations, it is said that they involve both contemplation and realization. Since one is currently still at the stage of noble contemplation (*ārya-darśana*) and has not yet attained them, why do you suddenly offer such praise?
Answer: Among the [eight], the first seven follow from contemplation; although one has not yet realized cessation (*nirodha*), this is merely stated from the perspective of the majority.

Furthermore, when asked what the meaning of liberation (*vimukti*) is, it refers to the sense of casting off, turning away from, and abandoning. It begins with the abandonment of the form and formless realms, and the abandonment of the mind and the mindless state; when both mind and form are forgotten, it culminates in cessation (*nirodha*), wherein even the conditioned mind that remains should be relinquished.
It is a pity that the Lesser Vehicle stops at this point.
As for the various non-existences that cannot be relinquished—who is it that relinquishes them?
When both subject and object are utterly severed and no dharma presents itself to the mind, this is certainly beyond their reach.

Furthermore, when asked what distinguishes the three bases—the "Universal," the "Superior," and so forth—the answer is as follows: because one perceives that there is something to be relinquished, that which is relinquished constitutes liberation.
Conversely, because one perceives a superior objective sphere, that which is capable of being superior constitutes the "Superior Base" (abhibhvāyatana).
Not only can it prevail, but it can also extensively transform all that is mind-only; since there is nowhere that is not blue or other such colors, what kind of object could it possibly be?
How could this not lead one to regard it as superior and form a saintly understanding (*ārya-saṃjñā*)?
To go beyond this is what constitutes goodness.

As for the "three wisdoms" (*tri-prajñā*), they refer to the successive advancement through hearing, reflection, and cultivation; as these serve as the gradual stages for entering the Path and are all capable of giving rise to wisdom, they collectively receive that name.
It can be understood by correlating them in their respective order; this differs from the case of Avalokiteśvara entering samādhi through hearing, contemplation, and cultivation, and so forth.
Regarding the sixteen truths, the four truths, and so on, when praised in terms of the gate of contemplating the truths, there are both general and specific aspects.
The dharmas of cause and effect, both mundane and supramundane, are summarized into four: namely, suffering, origin, cessation, and the path. When divided specifically into four types, they are:

arising and ceasing, non-arising, the immeasurable, and the unconditioned. These are discussed in terms of the skillful and the unskillful regarding the True and the Middle; because each is thoroughly real, they are called "truths" (*satya*).
If one were to analyze this exhaustively, the meaning would be inexhaustible.

For now, following the commentary, it is said that within the stage of patience (*kṣānti*), there are distinctions such as superior, middling, and inferior, as well as the universal contemplation (*parīkṣā*) and so forth, totaling sixteen aspects of the truths (*satya*). From the perspective of the practice itself, these are called "gates of contemplation" (*vipaśyanā-mukha*); from the perspective of the objects being contemplated, they are called "gates of the truths" (*satya-mukha*). Both refer to what has been explained above, and so forth.
Regarding the "contemplation in four, three, two, and one stages," this does not depart from praising the layperson's virtue by means of the four roots of goodness (*catur-kuśalamūla*).
From the stage of "Heat" (*uṣmagata*) up to the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*), there are differences between counting in reverse order and eliminating in forward order.

If one counts in reverse order, each preceding stage is added to each succeeding stage; if one eliminates in forward order, each succeeding stage is subtracted from each preceding stage, as can be understood from the text.
Alternatively, calculating from the four fruits starting from the last and moving backward is not the intended meaning here; therefore, the explanation follows the former method.

Regarding the attainment of the ninety *kṣāntis* (patiences), there were formerly three explanations, none of which is adopted here; instead, we now follow the formal and distinct concluding text of the sūtra.

From the twenty-second chapter downward, the various *dharmalakṣaṇas* (dharma-characteristics) together constitute eighty-one items; when combined with the nine [stages] such as the four *dhyānas*, they precisely total ninety *kṣāntis*.
Fortunately, there are clear texts, and these several principles are sufficient for practice; why seek anything else?
As for the general designation "patience" (kṣānti), it has no other meaning than simply being at peace with things as they are.
Since this is called a method for harmonizing the mind, what single method could exist that is not patience?

Among the enumerations of the heavens, when it is said that "ten thousand" (wan) is used as the upper term for the number, this merely means that ten thousand times ten thousand constitutes one hundred million (yi).

The other three versions differ in their overall structure, in the distinction between general and specific categories, and in their expansion or contraction; these differences can be understood by comparing them with the respective proofs.
Regarding the five heavens of Joyful Bliss (*Sukha*), the text presents two interpretations.
As for the "five factors" (*pañcāṅga*), these refer to the array of secondary qualities (*guṇa*) produced by the fourth dhyāna, and do not pertain to the number of heavens.
If one speaks of the "five pure abodes" (*pañca-śuddhāvāsa*), they refer precisely to the five *anāgāmin* heavens.
As for the mention of "joy and bliss," this is likewise a figurative expression.
These are the traces left by noble ones who have attained the third fruit, manifesting among the various devas; fundamentally, they have no fixed location.

This is what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* when it says: "Just as in this world, vast wildernesses and deep mountains that are sites for the sacred path are all maintained by Arhats, such that ordinary people of the world cannot see them."
The four successive dhyānas are listed here; for details, as stated in the *Abhidharmakośa* and so forth.

Regarding the "meditative attainments of the heavens" (*devasamāpatti*) and the "meditative attainments of the qualities" (*guṇasamāpatti*), as explained in the commentary, these refer to the two meanings of "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) and "retribution" (*vipāka*).
"Savoring" (āsvādana) refers to being attached to meditative concentration; it is precisely this state of being attached to the fundamental dhyānas that constitutes it.
If one is without attachment to dhyāna, it is called "pure dhyāna" (śuddha-dhyāna), as in the case of the sixfold contemplation, the eight noble lineages, and so forth.
The "lesser five desires" refers to such things as holding hands, laughing, and gazing;
if one speaks of the "six desires," it is from the perspective of their bases.
The "accomplishment of the four faiths" refers to faith in the Three Jewels and in the precepts; these constitute the four indestructible faiths, which are also called pure faiths.
Regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, there are five paths": in the general enumeration, sometimes only humans and devas are listed, as they are the vessels that receive the path;
alternatively, all five paths may be clearly explained, in which case asuras are omitted because ghosts and animals lack fixed forms.
If one speaks of the three wholesome, the three unwholesome, and the four destinies (*gati*), then the number of the six realms is complete, and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the sequence of priority among the six realms: humans and devas come first, followed by the three evil realms; as for the *asuras*, they may or may not be present, and thus their position in the sequence is not fixed.
Alternatively, because there were no conditions for them to encounter this sutra, they are not included in the enumerated list.

Regarding the mention of "assemblies from other regions" as those with "different views in other places," this means that within the assemblies of other regions, different perceptions are observed: either they see [beings] coming and going yet leave no trace of such movement; or they see those assemblies, without rising from their seats, arriving in this land to accomplish transformative deeds. All of these are variations of perception according to conditions, collectively demonstrating that the discourse on transformation is not different [from the original].

Furthermore, there are those who transform the pure lands of the ten directions; "transform" here refers to the "transformation of purity" found in the *Lotus Sūtra*, signifying the purification of the three lands.

Although the manifested pure appearances are without discrimination, from a general perspective based on phenomena, they are described in terms of the manifestation of the reward land (*saṃbhogakāya-bhūmi*); therefore, it is said that these are not the purity of the land of tranquil light (*prabhāsvara*).
In essence, the pure marks of the *jiguang* (quiescent light) realm are perceived solely by ultimate wisdom; they are not accessible to those in lower stages or to the transformed assemblies.
Furthermore, what is called the manifestation of ten billion high seats refers to the responsive form (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*) of the *Avataṃsaka*.
As for those upon the flowers, these are the hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of transformation bodies beneath the trees.
In reality, they are all within the realm of the Flower Treasury (Kusumatalagarbha); without moving or departing, they ascend and travel through it. Thus it is said, "and so forth."
The fact that the eight classes of great assemblies each sit upon precious flowers collectively manifests the inconceivable transformative activities of the principal and the retinue.

As for the Buddha and the great assembly each expounding Prajñāpāramitā, there are two kinds of Prajñā: the common and the uncommon. The common refers to this present sutra; the uncommon refers to the *Avataṃsaka*.
Although they differ in being shared or unshared, all are Prajñā.

Since all are Prajñā, there is likewise nothing that is not the Avataṃsaka; thus we know that the Buddha’s transformations are harmoniously integrated from the outset, with no distinction between self and other—it is only human sentiment that gives rise to divergent views.

Within this, eight groups are extracted; since each of the Four Heavenly Kings leads two assemblies, they constitute eight. Furthermore, various sutras list devas, nāgas, and others as these eight; in reality, they are all assemblies of Dharma protectors, and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "sitting on a nine-tiered seat" (*jiuji-pí-zuò*), according to the commentary, one should simply change "kalpa" (*jié*) to "tier" (*jí*), meaning a level or stage.
Since the current edition of the sutra has already been corrected, there is no need for further alteration.
Moreover, the character "kalpa" (劫) does not necessarily mean "grade" (級);

while it may be acceptable as a rough approximation, the multitude now assembled, each numbering several tens of thousands, is already inconceivable. How much more so when they have all come together and are each seated upon these thrones!
Furthermore, the assembly was nine hundred and fifty *li* wide; this too is merely stated according to the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
If it were inconceivable, how could it be limited to such a specific quantity?

Just as the room of Vimalakīrti could accommodate thirty-two thousand lion thrones, it is difficult to compare this with [ordinary space] by means of arguments regarding breadth, narrowness, superiority, or inferiority.
By this, we know that the Buddha’s transformations can only be understood through inconceivable logic; if one were to analyze them with ordinary sentiments, how could they not be deemed miraculous?
Nevertheless, for now, one cannot avoid saying that this is like a fool talking in his dreams.
The section beginning with "Questioning the various sutras" concerns the inquiry into the assembly of listeners, which is clear.

In the response, it is stated that while the retributions of the three realms may indeed be explained through karma, the distinction between having or not having the conditions to see the Buddha does not necessarily depend solely on good or evil; hence the phrase "as it is said... and so forth.
By analogy with cases such as hearing the Dharma versus not hearing the Dharma, this should also be understood.
Now, correcting this by means of a passage from the *Mahāvaipulya Sūtra*: laxity in the precepts is not necessarily an obstacle, whereas laxity in the vehicle (the Mahāyāna) is indeed an obstacle.
By means of the following two phrases, the doctrine of "conditioned" and "unconditioned" conditions attains its correct form.
One should further distinguish that each of the Vehicles (yāna) and Precepts (śīla) has three grades, and discuss their relative urgency through the four permutations, as in the text.
"Qian" (僉) means "all.

From the section "At that time, the Ten Epithets" onwards, Part Two: The Introductory Narrative of the Arousing of the Resolve.
The text consists of five parts.

Regarding the phrase "at that time" (*tadā*), it refers to the period immediately following the assembly of the multitude and preceding the manifestation of the auspicious signs; it denotes precisely this moment.
Regarding the "Ten Epithets" and so forth: these are the titles representing the ten thousand virtues of the Teacher.
They serve to inspire a heart of yearning and admiration among the assembly; thus, his virtue is supreme.
Briefly stated, there are four:

namely, the Ten Epithets, the Three Kinds of Knowledge, the Virtue of Wisdom, and the Virtue of Cessation; all titles of virtue are fully contained within these, each being mentioned according to its preeminence.
The names and characteristics of the ten titles are as explained in detail elsewhere, and so forth.
Regarding the virtues of wisdom and abandonment, they are as interpreted above, and so forth.
*Śākyamuni* is the specific title corresponding to the general title mentioned above; this is its particular distinction.
Śākya is his clan name, which here means "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren).
Muni is his personal name, which here means "Silent Stillness" (Jimo).
Being both benevolent and silent, he is one whose benevolent virtue is tranquil.
If one pursues this to its ultimate limit, the Way of the Buddha can be attained; as those who follow him, should we not strive for this?
In India there are generally four castes, and Śākyamuni belonged to the lineage of the Golden Wheel, namely the Kṣatriya.
Regarding other Brahmins and so forth, as detailed elsewhere, etc.:
as for the surnames of one's lineage, they may be Śākya, Gautama, Ikṣvāku, or others, differing according to the specific ancestral line from which one derives one's clan name.
The people returning as if to a marketplace is just as the Book of Documents says:
"In ancient times, when King Tai was dwelling in Bin, the Di people invaded him; he settled at Mount Qi, and those who followed him were like people returning to a marketplace. This is what it means.
In the eighth month of the first year, it was precisely when the Tathāgata was about to preach this sutra and manifested auspicious signs to initiate the teaching.
The commentary cites the judgment of Tripiṭaka Master Paramārtha, which does not exceed three points:

first, that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for forty-five years while in the world; second, that he assigned the turning of the three wheels of Dharma to these forty-five years; and third, that he distinguished between the simultaneous and sequential aspects of both the exoteric and esoteric teachings.
Now, based on the established doctrine of our own school, there are three points that cannot be altered, by which one may discern right from wrong.

First, it is universally agreed upon in both the sūtras and śāstras that the Tathāgata preached the Dharma for fifty years after attaining enlightenment; this is the first point that cannot be altered. Only the *Dvādaśayātra-sūtra* (The Sūtra of the Twelve Years’ Wandering) contains the claim that he attained enlightenment at thirty-five, which is merely a difference arising from the specific capacities and perspectives of those who perceived him.
Second, during the twelve years following his initial enlightenment, he taught the four Āgamas; this second point is unalterable.
Third, after the Prajñāpāramitā period, for eight years on Vulture Peak, he preached the Lotus Sūtra; this third point is unalterable.
By comparing this with that, the advance and retreat of the years can be clearly known.

As for the current claim that it was the eighth day of the first month, this must refer to the period immediately following the preaching of the various *Prajñāpāramitā* sūtras, when the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* (*Renwang jing*) was subsequently delivered.
As for the mention of the eighth day of the month, it is like the eighth day of the first lunar month; it is merely an abbreviation of the text.
"Just sitting" (fāng zuò) means "beginning to sit," which is also correct.
As for the Buddha’s original dwelling and the Dharma he realized himself, his dwelling therein has been long indeed.
As for the statement that they are "currently seated," it merely means that the manifest nature is cultivated to reveal the inherent nature.

The "Ten Grounds" (daśabhūmi) here are not the same as the ten grounds previously mentioned; as the commentary quotes from the *Tathāgatagarbha-sūtra* at length, these are the grounds upon which a Buddha dwells. They are analogous to the "ten non-sequential [grounds]" in the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which are not the sequential ten grounds.

As for the commentary’s explanation that this refers to the "separate teaching" connecting to the "teaching of commonality" and so forth, although there is some truth to this reasoning, it ultimately does not constitute a comprehensive argument; let us set it aside for now.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "entering the samādhi of the chamber of great quiescence," how could the stage previously dwelt upon be inconsistent with the principle of quiescence?
Generally speaking, that which was previously abiding in is wisdom (*jñāna*), while that which is now entering is meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Furthermore, all preaching of the Dharma necessarily has its proper sequence: one enters concentration and subsequently observes the capacities of sentient beings; having observed their capacities, one then initiates the teaching—this is the established order. Therefore, he now enters this concentration.
In general, this is elaborated through four points:

first, observing the faculties of others to administer the appropriate medicine; second, giving rise to wisdom based on meditative concentration; third, the ritual protocols for preaching the Dharma; and fourth, using the noble to illustrate the ordinary.
Having attained these four intentions, their essential meaning becomes clear.
They may also be correlated with the four *siddhāntas*, which is to say, the principle of *pratītyasamutpāda* (dependent origination), and so forth.
The section beginning with "Furthermore, great quiescence" is divided into two parts:

First, the explanation based on principle (*li*): Principle has "ultimate quiescence" as its meaning, and *nirvāṇa* is likewise a term for quiescence; therefore, it is explained by correlating it with the Great *Nirvāṇa* of the three virtues. That is to say, "Great" (*mahat*) refers to the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Quiescence" (*śama*) refers to Prajñā, and "Cessation" (*nirodha*) refers to Liberation (*vimukti*). Only when these three are fully possessed is it called "profound meditation" (*gambhīra-dhyāna*). To dwell in reliance upon this, there is nothing superior to it; thus, the "room" is used to symbolize it.
A "cave" (kū) is also a "chamber" (śālā); this is further corroborated by the citation of the passage on "entering the great chamber.
Moreover, the statement in the "Dharma Master Chapter" that "compassion is the chamber" is likewise consistent with this principle.
As for "Great Quiescence," its meaning is illumination.
Ultimate quiescence is itself illumination; it is illuminated while remaining eternally quiescent.
Because it is illuminated while eternally quiescent, even though there is movement, it is ever more quiescent, and thus its illumination is inexhaustible.
Being quiescent yet constantly illuminating, one speaks of illumination precisely through stillness; thus, its responsiveness is unimpeded.
This is like an empty room being able to contain things, or the capacity of *prajñā* (wisdom) to illuminate.
Next, regarding the manifestation through contemplation, the meaning corresponds to contemplating the mind.
The text first establishes the objective realm for contemplation.
The initial four lines refer to the emptiness of the chamber; fundamentally, this is a single objective realm.
Regarding the phrase "brightness and darkness differ," this establishes the contemplation of brightness in contrast to darkness.
Although brightness and darkness differ, the objective realm remains as it is.
The next four lines provide a brief summary of both the Dharma and the analogy, which can be understood accordingly.

The four lines following "The sun rises" correspond precisely to this: because wisdom arises, the objective realm becomes manifest, just as when the sun rises, the myriad phenomena are simultaneously illuminated;
because the darkness of delusion causes the mind to be obscured, it is likened to when the sun sets, and nothing at all can be seen.

It is also like the great void, which is fundamentally neither light nor darkness, yet light and darkness exclude one another; this is like the mutual overturning of delusion and wisdom, while the nature of reality remains eternally identical—this too is the meaning of "perfect" (yuan).

If brightness and darkness, though distinct, are by nature ever-pure, then this directly demonstrates the ultimate perfection through the essence of the inconceivable realm; that is to say, the non-interference between brightness and darkness reveals the Buddha’s Bodhi.
Therefore, the cited proofs state that although ignorance is defiled, its nature is itself clarity; not even a single dharma is lacking.
Thus, the claim that "all sentient beings are the very aspect of bodhi and cannot be further extinguished" is likely an error.
The text should read "attains" (得), though it may also be abbreviated; these variations merely clarify one another.
This is because that which is directly present is the very essence itself, such that not even a single hair’s breadth can be added to or subtracted from it.

Regarding "contemplating the radiance emitted from the objects of focus": if one interprets this through the lens of phenomenal activity, it simply means that the contemplation initiates the emission of light by taking the objects that can be traversed as its conditions;

in this sense, the meaning remains relatively proximate. Now, in this commentary, I explain it according to the ultimate principle, stating: "and so forth. This means that there is contemplation without contemplation, contemplating within the signless; there is focusing without an object, focusing upon the *dharmatā*. This is what constitutes the great bliss of self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*).
If the Dharma is fundamentally without marks, yet contemplating it gives rise to marks;
if its nature is fundamentally without conditions, yet conditioning it causes that nature to arise.
This being so, what is there to contemplate or to deliberate?
It was specifically for the sake of this karmic opportunity that [the Buddha] attained [this state] spontaneously;

he emitted light and manifested auspicious signs, causing the earth to quake in six ways, which gave rise to doubts among the multitude. King Prasenajit knew in his heart that this was so, and that only the Buddha could resolve it; yet, as the Tathāgata remained in meditative absorption, the King could not yet venture to request an audience. Thereupon, he played various kinds of exquisite music to alert the great assembly.
Consequently, the Tathāgata arose from meditative concentration and ascended the Dharma seat, after which the orthodox teaching was able to be inaugurated, as the sutra states at length.

Regarding the section beginning with "Questioning about the Formless Realm," it is a follow-up inquiry: since light must necessarily illuminate form, how can there be illumination in the formless realm?
The answer states that although there is no coarse form (*rūpa*), there is subtle form; this follows the logic of the question and its response.
However, if we discuss the Buddha’s radiance, it illuminates both existence and non-existence.
Indeed, the Buddha’s light fundamentally uses the illumination of the signless (*animitta*) to illuminate the formless forms; thus, the original question was likely mistaken.
As for the term "subtle form," it is visible only to the divine eye and is beyond the reach of the fleshly eye.

This statement that those of the two vehicles do not see it means that even though the wisdom-eye of the two vehicles illuminates emptiness, they still cannot perceive it; only by attaining the divine eye can one truly see it.

Furthermore, when the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states that "the form of the formless realm is not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas," this is spoken from the perspective that all phenomena are wondrously expressed; it does not refer to the sectarian tenets that claim the existence or non-existence of form in the formless realm is indeterminate as explained in the various treatises. Thus, these matters cannot be discussed in a single, uniform manner.
The phrase "emitting light to cause the consciousness to realize the root of wisdom" below indicates that this is not established in vain.
Light is rooted in wisdom; it is only through wisdom that one can emit light, and therefore wisdom is taken as the root.
The flower symbolizes the cause; since one can only obtain the fruit after the cause, the Path is taken as the cause.

Furthermore, the light is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) because it transforms according to the capacity of the recipient, while the flower is called "vision" (*darśana*) because it serves to establish a karmic connection (*pratyaya*). The corresponding explanations are thus clear.

Regarding the current statement that those who do not perceive the flower [do so] through "xiang" (相), "xiang" should be read as "xiang" (想). By distinguishing between the two benefits—the present and the future—the text achieves its literary elegance.
Furthermore, the previous explanation of the Manifestation of the Master’s Appearance belongs fundamentally to the aspect of response (*nirmāṇa*).
To say that there is "an awakening through conditions" and so forth refers entirely to the implicit meaning beyond the words regarding resonance and response.

Under the phrase "immeasurable transformations," it clarifies that the falling flowers involve both transformation and non-transformation: the "transformed" are the mental flowers, while the "non-transformed" are the external flowers.

Only the gods of the form and formless realms can undergo transformation because their meditative power is superior; the gods of the desire realm lack this capacity and thus are not said to transform—this fully exhausts the principle of the matter.
Furthermore, "kalpa" (劫) should be read as "grade" (級); it is merely an error resulting from phonetic corruption.

Regarding the phrase "the great earth trembles" (dàdì zhèndòng), "zhèn" should be corrected to "zhèn" (zhèndòng). This trembling has its conditions, its numerical categories, and its significance; six types constitute its number.
Regarding the conditions for movement (*iñjanā-pratyaya*), there are eight conditions each as set forth in the *Āgama* and the *Ekottarika-āgama*.
Regarding the movement of the mind (*iñjitamati*), it is explained as cited later from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*.

Regarding the phrase "shaking the earth so as to move the mind" and so forth: this applies not only to the phenomenal aspect but must also accord with principle; it is what the Chan school refers to in the "Wind and Banner" dialogue.
It is also like the ancient saying that the substance of the earth is fundamentally quiescent, and that movement necessarily entails change.
All of these are close approximations.

Among the eight conditions mentioned in the *Āgamas*, that which is called the "condition of ceasing instruction" refers to the time when one returns to the Truth and brings the transformative teachings to rest.
However, while ceasing instruction does not necessarily entail returning to the Truth, returning to the Truth necessarily entails ceasing instruction.
The remaining conditions may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the wind-circles moving upward and downward among the eight conditions in the *Ekottarika-āgama*, it is nothing other than the wind-circles and the winds of the four great elements striking one another, moving in succession.

"Movement must produce sound, and sound constitutes thunder; this is perhaps one interpretation. The character "one" (一) is missing from the text, and it is largely the same as, yet slightly different from, what was previously cited from the *Āgama*.

Regarding the statement in the *Dongyi* (Moving the Mind) that "one treats three kinds of afflictions," these are: first, greed; second, delusion; and third, pride. This is clear from the subsequent passage concerning rebirth in the heavens.

Regarding the eighteen unique qualities (*āveṇika-dharma*), there are versions derived from both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, which differ in their doctrinal characteristics (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) though they are identical in being "unique.

The passage beginning with "Previously, for my sake" below summarizes the scriptures previously mentioned.

Including the eight years thereafter when the *Lotus Sūtra* was preached, it is clear that he taught the Dharma for fifty years in total.
If it were different from the finger, then there would be an error in perception.
Second, "now" is doubtful; it constitutes two [points]: first, the present time; second, the doubt. Thus, there are two.
First, the initial presentation of the community's doubts is twofold:

As for the statement that the King’s clan name was Yue (Moon) and his personal name was Guang (Light), this need not necessarily be so; his original name was Prasenajit, and after entering the Way, his Dharma-name became Moonlight (Yueguang). In the second sequence of questions posed to the assembly, some refer only to two individuals, while others add the character "Dharma" (fǎ); the latter variation is more convenient.

Regarding the phrase "awakening the Tathāgata," "awakening" (*wù*) should be written as "awakening from sleep" (*wù*). The original scripture has already been corrected, but this [term] must be amended.

This present arrangement is merely a symbolic representation.

Subsequently, Bodhisattvas from the ten directions all arrived together to perform music, and it was likewise so.

From the passage "The Buddha knew the time" onwards, it clarifies that because of the aforementioned conditions of thought, the opportunity has been attained; thus, the time for preaching this present *prajñā* has arrived.
The "skilled physician" bestowing medicine, as well as the three karmas and the three wheels, can be understood through their combined interpretation.

In all ritual protocols, there is nothing that does not manifest the marks of the Reward Land (vipākabhūmi) as the body of the Honored One with Extraordinary Features; therefore, it is likened to the King of Mountains.

Regarding the teaching, one returns to the fundamental school, yet the essential meaning must be understood as distinct and direct; although the text follows the particular, the meaning necessarily encompasses the universal, and so forth.
